scene.testo: Fire in space can burn through a cabin in seconds. On November 2, 2000, the first crew arrived at the International Space Station. Since then, emergencies have never stopped. Here is how astronauts survived their worst moments, and what it cost them.

Imagine you are floating inside the station at 6 AM. You are about 250 miles above Earth. You are moving at 17,500 mph. Outside, the temperature swings between minus 250 and plus 250 degrees Fahrenheit. A thin wall protects you.

That wall is made of aluminum and layered shielding. Your whole world is a few hundred cubic feet of air. Everything you need to breathe, drink, and stay warm is made or recycled inside this one fragile shell.

Then an alarm sounds. A loud, harsh tone. Lights flash. Your heart jumps. In space, there is no fire department, no ambulance, and no exit door. The only help is the crew around you and the training in your head.

So how do astronauts survive moments like this? Three things keep them alive, and you will get all three in this video. The first one begins with a mission that nearly ended in tragedy before it even reached the Moon.
It is April 13, 1970. Apollo 13 is about 200,000 miles from Earth. That is roughly 8 times the distance around our planet. Three men are heading for the Moon. Then a loud bang shakes the spacecraft.

An oxygen tank in the service module has failed. NASA's investigation later traced the cause to damaged wiring inside the tank. A second tank was also affected. The spacecraft began losing oxygen and electrical power fast.

The crew could not land on the Moon anymore. The mission changed in minutes. The new goal was simple and brutal: get home alive. The three men moved into the lunar module, a craft built for two people for two days.

That small lander became their lifeboat. It had to support three men for about four days. Engineers on the ground worked out how to ration power and water. The crew cut almost everything electrical to save every watt.

Inside, it got cold. The crew reported temperatures dropping near freezing in the cabin. Water was limited. They slept little. Food was eaten cold. Yet they kept working, because every checklist step mattered for the trip home.

Then came a second danger. Carbon dioxide was building up in the lunar module. The filters were the wrong shape for the command module's air system. Square filters could not fit round openings. Without a fix, the crew could be poisoned.

Engineers on the ground built a fix from items the crew actually had on board. Plastic bags, cardboard, tape, and a spacesuit hose. They read the instructions to the astronauts step by step. The improvised adapter worked.

That is the first pillar of survival: the team on the ground. Mission control in Houston is not just a room of screens. It is hundreds of specialists who can test a fix on Earth before the crew tries it in space.

On April 17, 1970, the crew splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. All three men survived. The mission is often called a successful failure. They never reached the Moon, but they proved what training and teamwork can do.

Now imagine a different danger, one that happens in silence. You are floating in the station again. The air smells strange. A faint haze hangs in the module. Fire is the one emergency every astronaut fears most.

Fire behaves differently in microgravity. Flames do not rise. They form a rounded blob, because hot air does not climb without gravity. That can make fire hard to predict, and NASA still studies it with experiments on the station.

The most famous space fire happened aboard the Russian station Mir. On February 23, 1997, an oxygen-generating canister caught fire. The flame burned like a blowtorch. Thick smoke filled the station, and the crew had limited time.

The fire blocked the path to one of the two Soyuz escape capsules. Six people were aboard, including three Russian and one American crew members, plus visitors. The crew put on masks and fought the flames with fire extinguishers.

The fire burned for roughly 14 minutes, according to accounts of the incident. Everyone survived. But the station was filled with smoke for hours afterward. The crew cleaned the air and kept the mission going.

Today every station module carries fire detectors, portable extinguishers, and breathing masks. Crews practice fire drills on a regular schedule. The lesson from Mir was clear: always keep a clear path to your escape vehicle.

Here is the comparison with Earth. At home, you leave a burning building through a door. In orbit, your door is a capsule parked outside. Evacuation means a spacecraft, a hatch, and a fall through the atmosphere.

Next, imagine the sound of a hiss. On August 30, 2018, ground teams detected a slow drop in station air pressure. The leak was traced to a tiny hole, about 2 millimeters wide, in a docked Soyuz spacecraft.
That is smaller than a pencil. Yet air was slipping out. The crew was woken and the hole was found. They plugged it first with a finger, then with tape and a sealant. The pressure stabilized.

Why does a tiny hole matter? Because the station holds air at normal sea level pressure, about 14.7 pounds per square inch. Outside is a near perfect vacuum. A leak is a constant push outward, hour after hour.

Crews have a plan for bigger leaks. They can close hatches between modules and retreat to a safe section. Sensors track pressure all day. Even slow leaks are measured in hours, which gives the team time to respond.

That is the second pillar: redundancy. Critical systems have backups, and backups have backups. Air, power, cooling, and communications all have more than one path. Nothing on the station depends on a single point of failure.

Now step outside. Imagine you are on a spacewalk, floating about 250 miles above Earth. Your suit is a personal spacecraft. It holds air, water, power, and cooling. One small mistake out here can become a life-threatening problem.

On July 16, 2013, an astronaut named Luca Parmitano was on a spacewalk when water began collecting in his helmet. It was documented by NASA's investigation. At first it seemed small. Then it grew, and covered his eyes and nose.
He could not see well. He could barely hear. Water moved around his face because there was no gravity to pull it down. The walk was ended early, and he had to return to the airlock.

The crew inside pulled him in and removed his helmet. Investigators later found that a blockage in the suit's cooling system caused the water to spill into the helmet. About a pint and a half of water had gathered, according to NASA's report.

After that near miss, NASA added a snorkel-like breathing tube and absorbent pads inside the helmet. It is a small change with a big purpose. Every close call becomes a new rule, and a new piece of hardware.
Compare that to scuba diving. A diver can rise to the surface. An astronaut cannot. The safe place is an airlock, sometimes hundreds of feet away along a handrail, with a tether as the only lifeline.

The third pillar is training. Astronauts spend years practicing emergencies before they fly. They rehearse fires, leaks, and rescues in simulators and in giant pools. They repeat each procedure until it becomes a habit.

That pool is the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory near Houston. It holds about 6.2 million gallons of water. That is roughly nine Olympic-size swimming pools. Full-size station mockups sit on the bottom, ready for practice.
Now imagine the final test: coming home. You strap into a Soyuz capsule. It is about the size of a small car interior. Soon the engines fire, and the capsule drops from orbit toward the atmosphere.

Reentry heat reaches about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit outside the capsule. A heat shield takes the blast. Then parachutes open, and a last burst of rockets softens the landing on the steppe. It is a controlled crash.

Sometimes the return goes off script. In 2008, a Soyuz capsule came in on a steeper path than planned. The crew felt much higher gravity forces, and the capsule landed far from the target. Rescue teams found them.

The crew was fine. Recovery teams are always waiting, because even a normal landing can be rough. Helicopters and trucks stand by. Medical staff check each astronaut right at the capsule, before anyone walks.

Space Shuttle crews trained for emergencies too. In 1986 and 2003, two shuttle missions ended in tragedy, with the loss of all seven crew members each time. Those losses changed NASA's safety rules and its culture.

It is important to be honest here. Not every emergency ends well. Space is dangerous. Every safety rule on the station today was written because somebody learned a hard lesson, sometimes at a terrible cost.

Yet the record shows steady progress. The International Space Station has been continuously occupied since November 2, 2000. That is more than two decades of people living in orbit, solving problems as they appear.

So here are your three answers. One, a huge team on the ground that solves problems with the crew. Two, backups for nearly every critical system. Three, years of training until emergency steps become second nature.

Think about Apollo 13 again. The fix that saved three lives was made from plastic bags, cardboard, and tape. Not a miracle machine. Just clear thinking, a calm voice on the radio, and people who refused to give up.

Back on Earth, you rarely face a problem where the nearest help is 250 miles straight down. Astronauts do, every single day. Their safety comes from preparation, humility, and the willingness to learn from every close call.

And here is the most surprising detail. The tiny leak in 2018 was only 2 millimeters wide, yet it was taken seriously for days. In space, even the smallest hole is treated like a crisis, because it can grow.

Astronauts do not survive because space is safe. They survive because they respect how dangerous it is. If you want more stories from orbit, subscribe to Orbital Days, and watch the next video on screen now.

descrizione:
How did astronauts survive their most dangerous emergencies? This documentary explores real moments from space history, including the Apollo 13 oxygen tank failure, the 1997 fire aboard the Mir space station, the 2018 Soyuz leak on the International Space Station, and the 2013 spacewalk water-in-helmet incident. Every fact comes from NASA reports and astronaut accounts.

You will learn how mission control, backup systems, and years of training keep crews alive 250 miles above Earth. We compare each emergency to life on Earth, with units in miles, feet, mph, and degrees Fahrenheit.
